summary: Outpost Zero: Mission Trainer is a free browser game that teaches kids ages 7 to 12 how to run a Moon or Mars outpost. The player is the Outpost Commander of a four-person crew and must balance power, oxygen, water ice, food, and radiation shielding. Every choice costs something else: switching the lab off saves battery but loses science, sending the crew outside to build means radiation exposure, and a thicker regolith roof protects the crew but takes time to build. When something fails, a crisis clock starts, and asking Earth for help takes minutes on Mars, so players must decide on their own. The game has four graded lessons, a mission-control console, a score report, and an explained review of every decision. It uses real solar flare records from NASA's DONKI space weather database, so the radiation storms players face really happened. It runs in any browser with no download or account, which makes it easy for classrooms and families to use.
details:
What it does: Outpost Zero: Mission Trainer is a browser-based mission-control simulator for kids ages 7 to 12. The player is the Outpost Commander of a four-person crew on the Moon or Mars and keeps them alive by managing power, oxygen, water ice, food and radiation shielding. It has four graded lessons (power through the night, solar storm watch, distance matters, and a full mission), a console with live telemetry, a cutaway of the outpost, spacewalk (EVA) planning, a build menu, standard operating procedures, and a score report that explains every decision.

How it works: Nothing is free. Switching the lab off saves battery but loses science. Sending crew outside to mine or build exposes them to radiation. Piling regolith on the habitat roof blocks about 90% of solar storm particles but only about 35% of cosmic rays, and each layer costs work time. When equipment fails or a storm alert arrives, a crisis clock starts. The player can ask Mission Control, but the reply takes the real communication delay (about 1.3 seconds for the Moon, 3 to 22 minutes for Mars), so crews must often decide alone.

Real NASA data: In the full mission, the radiation storms come from real solar flare records in NASA's DONKI space weather database, requested through the NASA API. Each mission day matches one real day and each flare happens at its real time of day. Players can choose the May 2024 solar superstorm or the most recent days. If the live request fails, the game uses a labelled saved copy of real DONKI records. Background radiation uses published measurements (Mars about 0.67 mSv/day from NASA's Curiosity rover; Moon about 1.4 mSv/day from China's Chang'e-4 lander). Power, air, water, food and dose numbers are simplified for teaching and the game says so.

Benefits and impact: Kids experience why real planners must trade power, safety, science and time, and why distance from Earth changes decisions. It is free, needs no download or account, and works in a classroom or at home. Failure is explained, not punished, and random faults and two sites make it replayable.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page; NASA DONKI through the NASA Open APIs; scripted test players to check the balance. Creativity: we turned a long list of space facts into a trainer with graded objectives, delayed messages from Earth and an after-action review.

Factors we considered: age-appropriate language, few core systems, honest labels for real and simplified data, and no safe choice without a cost. We have not yet tested it with children and plan to.
